lesson.child_mission: A persuasive letter greets the reader, states the request, gives reasons and closes politely.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same strategy to an unfamiliar topic or audience, then compare the effect of two different choices.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Draft a greeting, one-sentence request and polite close for a letter about a classroom plant shelf.

FEEDBACK
Greeting: Dear Ms ... Request: Please approve a plant shelf. Close: Kind regards, ...

CHECK
Jumping straight to complaints without a clear request weakens the letter.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Write a full persuasive letter (120–160 words) to a real school role about a fair request. Include greeting, request, two reasons, closing. Label each part.

Write a short reflection describing one specific revision you made and why.
lesson.learning_intention: A persuasive letter greets the reader, states the request, gives reasons and closes politely.
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Write a full persuasive letter (120–160 words) to a real school role about a fair request. Include greeting, request, two reasons, closing. Label each part. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Sample: original example using persuasive letter on new material; names a specific word, source or choice and explains its effect.

Parent: Written model 2: Sample error: Jumping straight to complaints without a clear request weakens the letter.. Correction: Greeting: Dear Ms ... Request: Please approve a plant shelf. Close: Kind regards, .... Why it helps the audience is stated.

Parent: Likely misconception: Jumping straight to complaints without a clear request weakens the letter. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating persuasive letter on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with persuasive letter, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

Parent: Marking notes: Accept original work about persuasive letter with a specific supporting detail. Reject copied model wording with no new material. / Accept a misconception, a correction, and a purpose-linked reason for persuasive letter. Reject corrections that do not change the inaccurate idea..

teach_steps.explain:
A persuasive letter greets the reader, states the request, gives reasons and closes politely.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make decisions based on specific language evidence, rather than guess or copy someone else. Keep the meaning accurate and explain the choice.

HOW TO WORK
Read the original example and locate the words or actions that support the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Check your response against the feedback: did you address the same skill and show your reasoning? If a detail is uncertain, identify what would have to be checked. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than making the answer longer.
